name: Aisha Yilmaz

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for meeting me, Aisha. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. What you tell me is confidential, so feel free to say what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Could you start by describing a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run a loader underground at Deepwater, the gold mine past the river. It's a load-haul-dump machine, an LHD, basically a low, long bucket loader that scoops broken rock after a blast and carries it to the ore pass. I go down the decline at six, do my pre-start checks, and then it's mucking out stopes all shift, which means clearing the blasted rock out of the holes where we mine.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like that it takes skill to get close to the wall without scraping the machine, and the crew is good to me. I'm also the health and safety rep for our crew with the union, so I'm the one who says no when something's dodgy. What wears me out is the heat down on the lower levels and the money. I'm on the lower grade, my partner Tomas is an apprentice electrician, and we've got about three weeks of savings between us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fine, but don't relax. Even when tech flops, the company still finds ways to squeeze. I'd post that the real fight was always pay and safety, not robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think we'd be okay for a while. Deepwater has years of gold left and nobody's making loaders smarter than me in this picture. But okay isn't great when we're three weeks from broke and my partner earns apprentice money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going, keep doing my rep work, and push for the lower grade to get moved up a band at the next pay round. I'd keep using the AI chat thing now and then to tidy my safety reports, because it saves me an hour. And Tomas and I would start the savings jar again, twenty-five each a week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly settled. Just that background hum about money that never really goes away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned some loaders at Deepwater are already run remotely. How does that work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: There are two loaders on the bottom level that get driven from a control room on the surface, with cameras and a joystick, which we call tele-remote. The operators up there wear clean shirts and drink proper coffee. I haven't asked to train on it, because I wanted to see if it actually worked first, and it mostly does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the background hum about money, exactly?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our car's twelve years old and the gearbox is going, and that's about two thousand we don't have. If it dies, I'm getting a lift with the shift bus at five in the morning. It's not a crisis, but it sits there.

say: I'd say the real fight was always **pay and safety**, not robots.
I'd warn people that companies **still squeeze** even when the tech flops.
think: Deepwater has **years of gold** left, so my job looks safe here.
Being **three weeks** from broke means safe still isn't comfortable.
do: Push for the lower grade to move up **a pay band** next round.
Keep using an **AI chat tool** to tidy safety reports.
Restart the **savings jar** with Tomas at twenty-five each a week.
feel: Mostly **settled**, with a steady hum of **money worry**.
S0.quote: Okay isn't great when we're three weeks from broke and my partner earns apprentice money.
fieldNote: Aisha's job looks **secure**, but a failing **gearbox** shows how thin the household cushion is.
She already watches the **tele-remote loaders** and waits for proof before training.
Her union rep role makes **pay and safety** her frame, not technology.

steps.text: Keep running the loader and doing union safety rep work
Push for the lower grade to move up a pay band
Use the AI chat tool to tidy weekly safety reports
Save twenty-five each a week with Tomas for the gearbox

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the union needs to get ahead of this, not react. The planning and scheduling side will go to software, and then they'll push more tele-remote and driverless loaders. I'd want a deal on training before the first machine changes, not after.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think it means my job turns into a control room job, or it goes. The thinking work like shift planning and ordering spare parts goes first, but loaders running on their own aren't science fiction, they're already two levels below me. I'd rather be the one in the clean shirt in the control room than the one who gets the letter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd put my name down for tele-remote training this year, now that I've seen it work. I'd use my rep role to make sure the training is offered to everyone on the crew, not just the favourites. And I'd ask Tomas to finish his ticket fast, because an electrician who knows mining automation is going to be worth a lot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit nervous, a bit fired up. It's change I can see coming, which is better than the kind you can't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the training goes only to direct staff, and some of your crew are left out?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd make a fuss, properly, with the union organiser and a written complaint. There's Mick on my crew, he's 58 and doesn't read well, and he'd be the first left behind. I'd sit with him for the theory if I had to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said Tomas could be worth a lot. Is your household betting on him?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit, yeah, and I know that's risky. If my hours get cut while he's still on apprentice pay, we'd be in real trouble for a year or two. So I'd want to train up myself and not just hope his trade carries us.

say: I'd say the union must **get ahead** of automation, not react to it.
I'd want a **training deal** agreed before the first machine changes.
think: My job becomes a **control room** job, or it goes.
Driverless loaders are already **two levels below** me, not science fiction.
Leaning on Tomas's trade while he's on **apprentice pay** is risky.
do: Sign up for **tele-remote training** this year.
Use the rep role to get training offered to the **whole crew**.
Urge Tomas to finish his **electrical ticket** quickly.
feel: Nervous but **fired up**, because she can see this change coming.
S1.quote: I'd rather be the one in the clean shirt in the control room than the one who gets the letter.
fieldNote: Aisha moves once something is **proven**, and the tele-remote loaders have proven themselves.
Her union instinct goes to protecting **Mick**, an older crewmate who reads poorly.
She sees a gap: hours could shrink while Tomas is still on **apprentice pay**.

steps.text: Apply for tele-remote loader training at Deepwater this year
File a union complaint if training skips labour-hire or older crew
Help Tomas finish his electrical ticket faster

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the moment for government to show it works for people. Tax the companies that own the AI and the robots, and use it to keep mining towns alive. I'd be out with the union, at meetings, writing letters, the lot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be scared. By 2028 the planning and the control room side goes to AGI, so the clean shirt job I wanted might not even exist. Then around 2031 the robots can drive a loader underground better than me, and that's my whole trade gone at 32.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Right away, I'd stop any plans for a bigger rent or a second car. I'd do the tele-remote training anyway, because three years of decent pay is worth having. I'd push the union hard for a redundancy fund now, while the company still needs us, and I'd look at whether my safety rep work could become a proper inspector job with the regulator.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like the floor's moving under me. I'm not frozen, but I'm frightened.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why the inspector job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because someone has to check that robots underground are safe, and I'd hope that stays a human job for a while. I know the hazards, I've written the reports. People will want a person to sign off on what happens a kilometre down, even with AGI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you and Tomas do if both your jobs looked shaky at the same time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd probably move in with my mum for a year to save. Mum and I would drive each other mad, but it's free and it's near the city. Neither of us is too proud for that, which helps.

say: I'd say government must **tax the companies** that own the AI and robots.
I'd be out with the **union**, writing letters and going to meetings.
think: By 2028 the **control room** job I wanted might not exist.
Robots could drive a loader underground better than me by **2031**, at 32.
do: Do the **tele-remote training** anyway for three years of decent pay.
Push the union for a **redundancy fund** while the company still needs miners.
Look into becoming a **mine safety inspector** with the regulator.
feel: **Frightened**, but still moving rather than frozen.
S2.quote: People will want a person to sign off on what happens a kilometre down, even with AGI.
fieldNote: Aisha sees AGI hit the **control room** first, closing her planned escape route.
She uses the three-year robot gap to **earn and organise** rather than wait.
Moving in with her **mum** is a real fallback she'd accept without shame.

steps.text: Finish tele-remote loader training for three more years of pay
Push the union for a redundancy fund at Deepwater
Apply to train as a mine safety inspector with the regulator
Move in with her mum for a year to save

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got five years, so there's no excuse for a mess. The union, the company and government should sit down now and agree what happens to every miner at Deepwater. I'd say that at every meeting until people were sick of me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, loader driving still ends in this picture, just with a bit more runway for me to get a second skill in. The office side goes by 2031, and the robots underground come around 2034. The fast one didn't give me that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd start a part-time certificate in workplace health and safety, nights, because it builds on my rep work. I'd still take the tele-remote training if it came up. Tomas and I would try to build two months of savings by year two, which means no holiday and the old car till it drops.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but it feels like something I can work on. More like a big job than a disaster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Two months of savings is a big jump from three weeks. How realistic is that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not very, honestly. Maybe if I picked up overtime on the weekends and we stopped eating out. I'd probably get to five or six weeks, and that would still be the most we've ever had.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would AGI change how you do the safety rep work before it takes the loader?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably. I'd use it to check reports and compare incidents across mines, which would make me better at it. My worry is the company using the same tools to argue a robot is safer than us, and then we'd be arguing with a computer.

say: I'd say **five years** leaves no excuse for leaving miners in a mess.
I'd push for the union, company and government to **agree a plan** now.
think: Loader driving still ends, just with **more runway**.
There's time for a **second skill**, which the fast picture didn't allow.
do: Start a **night certificate** in workplace health and safety.
Aim for **two months** of savings by skipping holidays and eating out.
feel: Worried, but it feels like **a big job**, not a disaster.
S3.quote: Loader driving still ends in this picture, just with a bit more runway for me to get a second skill in.
fieldNote: Aisha plans around the **2034 robot date** and uses the gap for a safety qualification.
She admits her savings goal is **unrealistic** and lowers it herself.
She fears companies using AI to argue **robots are safer** than miners.

steps.text: Start a night certificate in workplace health and safety
Push the union and company to agree a plan for every miner
Pick up weekend overtime to reach six weeks of savings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift, so let's not waste it. I'd want every mine to have a written transition plan, with dates, and the union checking it every year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think I'd be alright. The thinking side goes by 2036 and the robots in 2039, and by then I'd be 40 with a safety qualification and a decade of rep work behind me. Tomas would be a fully qualified electrician by then too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep driving the loader for now, because it pays and I'm good at it. I'd do the safety certificate slowly over two years, then go for a supervisor or safety officer role at Deepwater. I'd also start using AI properly for the rep work, not just now and then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calmer, though not totally. Ten years feels like enough to land on my feet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would still worry you, even with ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The money in the meantime. A lot can go wrong in ten years, like a layoff when gold drops or one of us getting hurt. With three weeks of savings, robots aren't the only thing that can knock us over.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you think about kids differently in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd probably still wait, like we are now, but for money reasons, not robots. Tomas wants kids by 32 and I'm less sure. Ten years of warning is about the one thing that would make me feel okay bringing a kid into this.

say: I'd say **ten years** is a gift we shouldn't waste.
I'd want every mine to publish a **transition plan** with dates.
think: By 2039 I'd be 40 with a **safety qualification** and years of rep work.
Tomas would be a **qualified electrician**, so the household would be steadier.
Layoffs or injuries could still hurt us when we have **three weeks** saved.
do: Keep **driving the loader** for the pay while studying.
Finish the **safety certificate** over two years.
Apply for a **safety officer** role at Deepwater afterwards.
feel: Calmer, with a sense she could **land on her feet**.
S4.quote: With three weeks of savings, robots aren't the only thing that can knock us over.
fieldNote: With ten years Aisha builds a clear **safety career** path out of loader driving.
Her mood stays **anxious** because the thin cushion, not AGI, is the near danger.
She links the warning time to whether to have **kids** at all.

steps.text: Keep driving the loader at Deepwater while studying
Finish the workplace health and safety certificate over two years
Use AI tools every week to compare incident reports
Apply for a safety officer role at Deepwater

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. The control room jobs and the loader jobs go within three years of each other, so there's nowhere to step sideways. What would help is training paid for by the company, in work time, and a proper redundancy fund that labour-hire and older miners can use too.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Safety. Everyone talks about jobs, but nobody asks who's checking the robots a kilometre underground. If the machines go in and the safety reps go out, someone's going to die a kilometre underground.

headlineQuote: If the machines go in and the safety reps go out, someone's going to die a kilometre underground.
portrait: Aisha, 27, runs an underground **loader** at Deepwater gold mine and is her crew's **union safety rep**.
She and her apprentice-electrician partner Tomas have about **three weeks** of savings.
She trusts change once it's **proven** and plans tele-remote and safety training.
Her mood runs from uneasy in AI Plateau to **alarmed** in the two faster AGI pictures.
With ten years she sees a path into a **safety officer** role.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because **control room** and loader jobs vanish within three years of each other.
whatWouldHelp: Company-paid **training** in work time, open to labour-hire and older miners.
A **redundancy fund** set up while miners still have bargaining power.
